34 Photo Booth Prop Ideas That Actually Work

Props exist to give your hands something to do. That is the whole mechanism, and it explains why a coffee cup outperforms most things sold as photo booth props.

Kishan Naik
July 26, 2026 6 min read

In this article

  1. What makes a good prop
  2. Twelve props already in your house
  3. Ten props worth actually buying
  4. Seven props for couples
  5. Five props for a solo session
  6. Why props on sticks do not work
  7. Running a prop box at an event
  8. The one rule that matters

Props exist for one reason: they give your hands something to do. Almost everyone who freezes in front of a camera freezes from the wrists down first - arms go stiff, hands hover somewhere near the hips, and the whole body follows into a kind of polite paralysis.

Hand someone an object and the problem disappears. They hold it, they look at it, they do something stupid with it, and the pose happens by itself. This is why photo booth props work, and it is also why the expensive ones on sticks work worse than a coffee cup.

What follows is 34 props sorted by where you would find them, from the kitchen drawer to a proper prop box, plus the rules for what makes a prop good.

What makes a good prop

  • It survives four frames. A one-joke prop is funny in frame one and dead by frame three. Something you can hold, wear, share and hide behind lasts the whole strip.
  • It sits above the shoulders. Booth crops are tight. Anything held at waist height is out of shot.
  • It does not hide the face. Full masks are the classic mistake - you get four frames of a mask and none of the person. Half-obscuring is better than fully.
  • It reads at 2 inches. Printed strips are small. Fine detail and small text disappear entirely.
  • It is not on a stick. More on that below.

The single best prop is something the person already brought with them - their drink, their glasses, their phone, their bag. It looks natural because it is, and there is no fumbling.

Twelve props already in your house

Nothing here needs buying. All of it is within thirty seconds of wherever you are sitting.

1A mug or a glass

Two people, two mugs, a toast in frame one and a drink in frame two. The most reliable prop there is, and it makes any strip look like a real morning rather than a staged one.

2Sunglasses

Wear them, share one lens each, push them up into your hair, put them on someone else. Four frames from one object.

3A blanket or throw

Two people under one blanket is the warmest-looking frame you can produce, and it hides the fact that neither of you knows what to do with your arms.

4A houseplant

Hold it in front of your face. Peer through the leaves. Absurd, photographs beautifully, and every home has one.

5A book

Reading intently while everything else goes wrong around you is a four-frame narrative on its own.

6Fairy lights

Wrap them round both of you. They give the strip a light source and a shape at the same time, which is rare in a prop.

7A hat - any hat

Swap it between frames. The continuity break makes a strip feel like it covers time rather than one moment.

8A pet

Unreliable, uncooperative, and the resulting strip will be the one you keep. A cat leaving the frame in image three is better than anything you could plan.

9A phone showing something

Hold up a photo of the person who could not be there, or a picture of the same group ten years ago.

10A tea towel

As a cape, a headscarf, a bandit mask, a blindfold. The most versatile object in any kitchen.

11Snacks

Mid-bite is an underrated expression. It is impossible to look self-conscious with a mouthful of crisps.

12A mirror or a phone screen

Angle it to catch a second face. Works particularly well in black and white.

Ten props worth actually buying

If you are building a box for a party or an event, this is the list that earns its space.

13Oversized novelty glasses

Heart-shaped, star-shaped, giant round frames. They read instantly at small print sizes, which is more than can be said for most bought props.

14Feather boas

Dated, slightly ridiculous, and they work every single time. They also solve the arm problem completely.

15Party hats and paper crowns

Cheap, stackable, and they sit exactly where a booth crop can see them.

16A small chalkboard or whiteboard

Guests write their own message. At a wedding this quietly becomes the guest book.

17Confetti

Throw it up in frame one, catch it falling in frames two and three. The best motion prop there is. Buy the biodegradable kind and accept that you will be finding it for weeks.

18A flower crown

Photographs far better than it has any right to, especially in colour.

19Wigs

The highest-impact prop per pound spent. A group where everyone swaps wigs between frames produces chaos of exactly the right kind.

20Fake moustaches - but self-adhesive

The stick-mounted ones are the single worst prop in circulation. Adhesive ones free both hands and stay put.

21A disposable camera

Holding a camera in a photo is a good visual joke, and it doubles as a genuine second camera for the evening.

22Umbrellas

Indoors, superstition aside, an open umbrella fills the frame and gives two people a reason to stand close.

Seven props for couples

23One scarf, two people

Wrapped around both necks. Forces you together and looks deliberate.

24A single pair of headphones, split

One earbud each. Reads instantly as a shared moment without needing an explanation.

25Something from your first date

A ticket stub, a receipt, a menu. Nobody looking at the strip will understand it and you will both remember exactly.

26A hand-lettered sign

One word per frame, spelling out a sentence across all four. The most-copied idea on this list, for good reason.

27Two disposable coffee cups

Clink them in frame one. The universal shorthand for a good ordinary day.

28A shared jumper

Both of you inside one oversized jumper. Ridiculous, warm, extremely photogenic.

29Your rings, held to the lens

For anniversaries and engagements - the only prop on this list that works better in close-up than at arm's length.

More ideas for two people specifically are in the 25 pose ideas, which covers what to do once you are holding something.

Five props for a solo session

Alone, props do more work, because there is no second person to react to. The prop becomes your scene partner.

30A mirror

Hold it at an angle so the strip shows your face twice, from two directions.

31The book you are actually reading

A dated record of what you were into. In two years this is the detail you will notice.

32Your keys, your bag, your everyday objects

An unglamorous, accurate portrait of a specific period of your life. These change more than you expect.

33A single flower

Held to the lens, tucked behind an ear, hiding half your face. It fills a frame that would otherwise be empty.

34Nothing at all - but move

The strongest solo strips often use no prop. Turn your head between frames, look off to one side, then straight down the lens. Movement replaces the prop entirely.

There is a full guide to shooting alone in solo photo booth ideas.

Why props on sticks do not work

Every event prop kit is full of cardboard shapes glued to wooden dowels. They are the default and they are the worst option available, for three reasons.

They occupy a hand permanently. The reason props help is that they solve the hands problem. A stick prop replaces the problem with a different one - now you are a person holding a stick.

They sit in front of the face. Held naturally, a stick prop covers the mouth. Four frames of a cardboard moustache is four frames of cardboard.

They flatten the image. A cardboard shape held at arm's length is on a different plane from the face, so it is either out of focus or it makes the face look out of focus.

Wearable props do all the same work while leaving your hands free. If you are buying for an event, buy things that go on people rather than things people hold up.

Running a prop box at an event

  • One shallow open box, not a deep one. People will not dig. Anything below the top layer is never used.
  • Twelve to fifteen items maximum. More than that and guests spend the whole session choosing instead of shooting.
  • Put it beside the booth, not behind it. If people have to walk away to get a prop, they will not.
  • Refresh it halfway through. Swap in five new things at the midpoint and the second half of the evening produces completely different strips.
  • Have wipes. Everyone will try on the same sunglasses. This is not a small consideration.

For occasion-specific prop kits, the wedding guide and the Halloween guide both include lists tuned to those events.

The one rule that matters

Use the prop to start, then forget about it. The best frame in almost any strip is the one where the prop has been abandoned mid-air and everyone is just laughing at what happened in the previous frame.

Props are a way in, not the point. They exist to get you past the first awkward three seconds. Once you are past that, the strip takes care of itself.

Grab something off the desk in front of you and open the booth. That is the entire preparation required.

Grab something off your desk and try it.

Frequently Asked Questions

What makes a good photo booth prop?

It has to survive four frames rather than being a single joke, sit above the shoulders where the crop can see it, avoid covering the face entirely, and stay legible at 2 inches wide on a printed strip. Objects you can hold, wear, share and hide behind meet all four.

What can I use as photo booth props at home?

Mugs, sunglasses, a blanket, a houseplant, a book, fairy lights, a hat, a tea towel, snacks and your pet all work well and are within thirty seconds of most sofas. Household objects usually photograph better than bought props because holding them looks natural.

Why are stick props a bad idea?

They permanently occupy a hand, which defeats the point of a prop; held naturally they cover the mouth; and because they sit on a different focal plane from the face, either the prop or the face ends up soft. Wearable props do the same job and leave both hands free.

How many props should I put out at a party?

Twelve to fifteen in one shallow open box beside the booth. More than that and guests spend the session choosing instead of shooting, and anything below the top layer of a deep box is never found at all.

What props work for a solo photo strip?

A mirror held at an angle, the book you are actually reading, your everyday objects, or a single flower. Alone, the prop has to act as your scene partner - though the strongest solo strips often use no prop at all and rely on movement between frames instead.

What are the best photo booth props for a virtual date or video call?

Props you both already have at home work best: matching coffee mugs, favorite sunglasses, books, or small handwritten messages. Because both participants appear on the same finished strip, matching everyday items visually connect both sides of the call.
